pairs.distinction: Climate change is the planet heating up over decades; dirty air is what I breathe in my own neighborhood today.
pairs.reason: Someone near a highway or a refinery and someone worried about global heating are naming different things, even when the same fuel causes both.

pairs.distinction: Disasters are floods, fires, storms and heat I'm living through now; climate change is the worry about where the planet is heading.
pairs.reason: A person rebuilding after a flood and a person anxious about the future would each pick one without thinking twice.

pairs.distinction: Losing nature is fewer birds, trees and green spaces near me, often from building and paving; climate change is global heating.
pairs.reason: Most nature loss people notice comes from development rather than heat, so the two point to different fixes.

pairs.distinction: On the personal page, getting around is my own trouble reaching places; on the societal page, needing a car is how towns are built.
pairs.reason: The same struggle shows up as a personal problem and as a design of places, so it belongs on both pages as two linked pains.

pairs.distinction: Infrastructure is roads, water and power breaking down; needing a car is having no other way to travel even when the roads work.
pairs.reason: Potholes and a missing bus line are different complaints, and a person would know which one they mean.

pairs.distinction: Kids' future is the fear that the next generation will have it worse for many reasons; climate change is one specific reason.
pairs.reason: Climate is one of several worries behind a fear for kids' future, so folding them together would lose both.
